J-L: Full-length X-rays of both lower extremities (J) and spine radiographs (K, L) of the proband in Family 4. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Sagittal T2 MRI in neutral position from a disease-focused SEDC article showing craniocervical instability; in-text documents atlanto-dens interval widening and C1 hypoplasia, classic SEDC craniovertebral manifestations. B: Flexion T2 MRI demonstrating dynamic atlantoaxial instability with atlanto-dens interval widening to 5mm and cord compression, a classic SEDC craniocervical manifestation in a disease-focused article. C: Extension T2 MRI showing persistent craniocervical instability with cord compression and T2 signal change of early myelopathy, classic SEDC complications in a disease-focused article.

findings.label: Pear-shaped vertebral bodies
findings.evidence: Caption: 'significant platyspondyly' (platyspondyly with pear-shaped vertebral bodies); visible flattened vertebral bodies on the babygram

panels.rationale: Single-panel babygram radiograph of a human patient at birth, explicitly captioned as showing spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita findings (significant platyspondyly, shortening of long bones with ragged metaphyses, mild iliac hypoplasia, delayed femoral head ossification). The disease-focused article title ('A novel mutation in the C-propeptide of COL2A1 causes atypical spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita') and in-text statement ('we diagnosed this patient as having atypical SEDC (Figure 1)') directly tie this figure to SEDC, including its atypical designation (absence of pubic ossification delay). No diagrams, controls, other diseases, or third-party copyright are involved. [raw subtype: atypical]

panels.figure_caption: Despite the widespread use and increasing availability of molecular genetic testing, clinical and radiographic diagnosis of skeletal dysplasias remains essential. New radiographic phenomena continue to be described, particularly in rare skeletal diseases in children. The use of mnemonic aids and recognizable visual patterns greatly facilitates differential diagnosis [1]. Pelvic radiography is a valuable imaging modality for screening and characterizing skeletal dysplasias, called “window to skeletal dysplasias” [2]. Congenital spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia or spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita (SEDC) is a part of the group of COL2A1-associated disorders, caused by pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene, encoding the alpha-1 chain of type II collagen. In typical cases, it manifests with disproportionate short stature, abnormal epiphyses, and flattened vertebral bodies with manifestations presented at birth [3]. Key radiographic manifestations of SEDC in infancy include delayed ossification of the skeleton with absence of the ossification centers of the pubic bones and knee epiphyses, and defective ossification of the vertebral bodies of the upper cervical spine, as well as small, dorsally wedged vertebral bodies of the thoracolumbar spine, and delayed ossification of the sacrum. In childhood, radiographic findings include retarded ossification of the pelvis with horizontal acetabular roofs, absent or retarded ossification of the femoral head and neck, coxa vara (decreased angle between the partly ossified or anticipated femoral neck and the femoral shaft), varying degrees of epiphyseal and metaphyseal abnormalities of the long tubular bones, and delayed appearance of the carpal and tarsal ossification centers [4]. However, most of these signs can also be observed in other dysplasias and as normal variants; therefore, a combination of radiographic features is necessary to verify the diagnosis. In analyzing the radiographs of patients with COL2A1-associated skeletal dysplasias, we noted a characteristic feature of pelvic bone contours in children with SEDC. The radiographs were evaluated by consensus among all co-authors—orthopedic surgeons (V.K and E.M.), skeletal radiologists (G.N. and Y.T.), and clinical geneticists (T.M. and D.G.). Formal interobserver agreement was not calculated because of the descriptive nature of the article. The lines outlining the inferior contour of the ilium can be compared to the outline of a flying dove (a). We propose to refer to this as the “dove drawing” sign. The “dove drawing” is composed of the inner spur (resembling the dove’s beak), formed by the inferior contour of the iliac part of the sciatic notch, sharply angled to the most medial contour of the iliac part of triradiate cartilage (marked in blue). The drawing continues laterally with the convex line (resembling the dove’s breast) composed of the lateral segment of the triradiate cartilage and medial segment of the acetabulum (marked in red), and the outer spur (resembling the junction between the body and wing) corresponding to the lateral part of the acetabulum and acetabular edge (marked in green) (b). This continuous line is demonstrated on the anteroposterior radiographs of 1-year-old (c) and 3-year-old (d) children with SEDC. Radiographs in the present report are partly overlapped with the authors’ previous publication [5] with principally different anatomical accents. In the typically developing children, neither the inner nor outer spur is seen, and the acetabular roof is concave. The outer and inner spurs of the “dove drawing” may hypothetically correspond to the metaphyseal corner spurs of long bones that are commonly seen in type 2 collagenopathy [6], although the connection between abnormal COL2A1 and these radiographic features is not clearly understood. The convexity of the triradiate cartilage segment and acetabulum is similar to the convexity of the bone ends seen in type 2 collagenopathy, particularly Kniest dysplasia and Stickler dysplasia [7], which may reflect a broader COL2A1-related skeletal phenotype rather than being specific to SEDC. Pelvic radiography is one of the most informative methods for screening skeletal dysplasias. Striking and memorable semiotic signs are widely known in clinical practice (for example, the “trident sign” in achondroplasia, caused by the endochondral ossification features of the iliac bones [8], multiple or “absent” ossification of the pubic bones in SEDC or cleidocranial dysplasia respectively [5,9]). The “dove drawing” sign may serve as an additional diagnostic clue, facilitating recognition of SEDC during routine radiographic evaluation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is a patient MRI showing neutral positioning, illustrating the anatomical context of the craniocervical instability characteristic of Spondyloepiphyseal Dysplasia Congenita, which is the topic of the figure. B: Panel B is a patient MRI showing flexion, illustrating the dynamic spinal cord compression and joint laxity specific to Spondyloepiphyseal Dysplasia Congenita. C: Panel C is a patient MRI showing extension, completing the documentation of dynamic instability and spinal cord compression in this case of Spondyloepiphyseal Dysplasia Congenita.

panels.figure_caption: Preoperative T2 weighted MRI sagittal sequences demonstrating dynamic instability and compression of the upper cervical spinal cord on flexion and extension positioning (arrow demonstrating site of maximal compression). A: Neutral Position, B: Flexion, C: Extension.
in_text_mentions: unassisted. The physical exam was normal without signs of myelopathy. Sleep studies were reviewed, which showed mixed sleep apnea with a more prominent central component. At this point, flexion-extension MRI was recommended. Flexion-extension MRI revealed a hypoplastic C1 vertebra and significant craniocervical joint laxity leading to substantial spinal canal narrowing at C1/C2 (6.5mm in flexion, 10mm in neutral and extension). Flexion views demonstrated circumferential loss of cerebrospinal fluid signal in this area. There was no appreciable change in spinal cord T2 signal change (Figure 3).
